A thing that I noticed in Kazakhstan was that there are Instagram pages dedicated to spreading information about events and activities that are going on around the city, including book clubs, master classes on drawing, etc. Friends and coworkers also go to cafes together.  Tbh I felt way less lonely because of the variety of activities that were offered, but the fact that some of these things allowed you to meet people even if you don't become friends with them. 

Here in the US, there are things to do outside of the house and social media, but I do feel like that the amount of things to do is not as much and\or are not advertised much on platforms that younger people are on. Part of that could be blamed on the algorithm on Instagram, but I also think that there is something else to this issue.

I would also like to add that I think Kazakhstan is also trying to ban social media for teenagers, which I also would be interesting to monitor, considering Dr. Ali Mattu's argument and the fact that teenagers in Kazakhstan (and Kazakhstanis in general) use social media for communication (mainly use Telegram, WhatsApp, and Instagram).

comments.text: A point that I think was brushed past a bit is just how little kids are allowed to do anymore. Most of us are raised by gen x who grew up with the "do you know where your children are?" ads, and in response to the danger of their upbringing and what would likely be considered neglect these days, they're on average much more restrictive than any previous generation. As a 2001 baby, I was never allowed to just go out by myself and play with a friend in the neighborhood until I was probably a teenager or close to it. I stopped asking to hang out with friends on the weekends because I knew either I couldn't because my parents didn't know the friends parents, or they were too busy to drive me and me walking a half mile down the sidewalk would be unthinkable, etc. Now I'm hearing that even the sleepover is going extinct, and while I understand the very valid fears parents have, I feel that from a very young age I was denied the opportunity to build connections in the ways previous generations could, and to build the habit of building those connections, so by the time some of those restrictions were lifted I didn't even know I wanted anything different, or where to start. It's hard to find third spaces, or deal with judgement from adults just for existing as a young person, but it's even harder to try and figure out how to work around that if the groundwork was never layed.

As a zillennial (Older Gen Z that doesn’t feel like they’re quite fit into either category) it’s been quite disheartening to come into adulthood during such a turbulent time. A lot of these issues were already impacting millennials, but the pandemic, generative AI, and a fascist takeover has amplified everything exponentially.

2020 was my senior year of high school and I am still fighting to reconnect with my friends from high school after we were so isolated for a very pivotal developmental stage. It’s natural for everyone to go their separate ways after high school, but I don’t feel like we really got to say goodbye. 

It makes me tear up, just thinking about the senior milestones—like prom, seeing your parents’ proud faces during graduation, and one last marching band performance/football game—that we had all looked forward to.

None of us really know what to do career-wise. The stories we were told as children by the school system and our parents are no longer applicable in a world hellbent on embracing generative AI over actual human innovation and creativity. 

Entry-level jobs are nonexistent and the places that are hiring have extreme turnover due to below living wages and toxic work environments. If you walk into a business to ask if they’re hiring, 9/10 times they will tell you to apply online where your resume gets buried under thousands of ai-generated applications on jobs that don’t even exist. 

Our parents, grandparents, and other older mentors have no idea how to help us because the societal landscape has shifted so dramatically from when they were young. College degrees mean nothing and most companies aren’t willing to take on the burden of training an inexperienced young hire. 

All I wish is to simply stop living through “unprecedented” times, but in the meantime it really helps to hear support from older generations who care. The best we can do is try to pick pathways that will still be around for decades to come and build up supportive and close-knit communities. 

If you are Gen Z and miss your old friends but worry they don’t feel the same, just send that quick DM. I’m proud to say that I get to go to my local pride event this year with two highschool friends I hadn’t spoken to for nearly 5 years. 

Also please use your internet research skills to find organizations in your area that can help you access the resources you need to survive. I waited WAY too long to apply for SNAP and other government-funded resources in my area. If your government has gutted those programs, look into local grass-roots organizations, mutual aid coalitions, and buy-nothing groups. I'm so happy you guys talked about preventative psychiatric care. It seems so taboo, even among doctors in my experience. All we ever hear is that we must be accepting of disabilities and learn to live with them. I never really thought that was the whole picture, so as a parent of a kid that started to show some strong signs of autism(at least I think based on what I know about it), I took it upon myself to do what I think the #1 job of a parent is- to raise a kid to be the best version of an adult that they can possibly be. My son had obsessive ticks and was very awkward and nervous socially. Any time I would ask a doctor about it, they would pretty much either waive it off or try to give me ways to cope with it.
I chose to do something different that got a lot of pushback.
I hounded him about his ticks. I let him know it was weird and that normal people don't do that. I worked with him to find solutions to kick one tick after another until they became less awkward, less frequent, and eventually gone. I worked with his sensory sensitivities through exposure. He hated it, but now he is glad that he isn't repulsed by paper, towels, and other materials. And I don't know if saying he was "repulsed" to feel those materials is the best way to describe how he felt, but it seems right to me as someone who hasn't felt whatever that is he was feeling. I've also worked very hard on his social anxieties by forcing him out of his comfort zone as much as possible. I've made him play sports, took him to concerts, festivals, and other events all against his will to help him feel more comfortable around strangers and crowds and to teach him to cope with discomforts.
 He's now a teenager and is such a functional, well-liked member of the community. Some of those traits he showed when he was younger are still somewhat present in him, especially his avoidance of the public, but it is to so much of a lesser degree than I think it could have been had I not chosen not to fully accept it as who he was destined to be. He is very fond of most people, but people love him because he has learned the correct way to act around them, even if what he expresses isn't in alignment with his true feelings. The point is- he comes off as very normal now, and I don't think that would be the case had I not chosen to push him, sometimes very painstakingly, toward normalcy. 
And if anybody reading this doesn't already think I'm an ignorant monster, I'll have you know I also took a similar approach with his vision. He was prescribed glasses at 3 years old. Being the idiot people think I am, I didn't like the idea of putting glasses on a 3 year old. I saw it as a crutch that could possibly weaken his eyesight. Young bodies are remarkable at correcting themselves, and I had a hunch that forcing him to use the eyes he had might strengthen them. Now don't get me wrong, I wouldn't have withheld glasses from him forever or had I felt he really needed them for safety or reading. I was prepared to do it for a few years though to see if his vision improved. Once he started kindergarten I sent his glasses with him to school in case he needed them, but told him to only use them if he really had to. Luckily he never liked wearing them either, so it didn't take much work on my part to get him to give his eyes a chance. I don't remember how long it took for his vision to improve, but I do know that at his most recent check-up he had better than 20/20 vision. I expect that wouldn't be the case had he been wearing corrective lenses since he was a toddler. 
I know what I've done with my son will not work in every situation. I think like the Dr said though, if you catch it at the right time, you can often veer it in a different direction that will lead to a much higher quality of life for people. I think that should be talked about and recommended more and shouldn't be seen as taboo. Parents, doctors, and society would do better by these people if they realize that sometimes the most compassionate thing for them is actually trying to cure them as much as possible instead of being resigned to believe that  of loading them up on drugs and being "accepting" of their illness is the only path forward.
